knowledge_points.label: Supplement: the policy-gradient form E[coef · ∇log π] and why a baseline is free
knowledge_points.statement: Every method in the paper updates θ along E[(1/|o|) Σ_t c_t ∇_θ log π_θ(o_t | q, o_<t)]: a per-token scalar coefficient times the score function, and subtracting any quantity that does not depend on the sampled output from c_t leaves the expected gradient unchanged while lowering its variance.

anchors.quote: Generally, the gradient with respect to the parameter $\theta$ of a training method can be written as:
during RL training, the value function is treated as a baseline in the calculation of the advantage for variance reduction
Attempt 1: Policy gradients (variances are too high)
Baselining: We can subtract any state-dependent term from our rewards

provenance.filtering_note: The paper writes the unified gradient (Eq. 5) and calls the value function a baseline, but never states the baseline identity E[b ∇log π] = 0 that justifies subtracting the group mean. The course does state it (p22, Sutton and Barto) and then notes that dividing by the std is not covered by it (p23). Added as an assumed prerequisite; basis inference.

external_prerequisites.note: same identity, stated as REINFORCE on slide p5

misconceptions.belief: Subtracting a baseline changes which direction the policy moves in expectation.
misconceptions.why_wrong: E_{o~π}[b ∇log π(o)] = b ∇ Σ_o π(o) = b ∇1 = 0 for any b that does not depend on o; only the variance changes.

misconceptions.belief: Any rescaling of the coefficient is equally harmless.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Dividing by a quantity that depends on the sampled group (the group std) changes the weighting of questions and is not covered by the identity; the course flags exactly this on p23.

predict.q: A question has two possible outputs with π(a) = 0.75, π(b) = 0.25 and rewards R(a) = 1, R(b) = 0. Write the expected policy gradient E[R ∇log π] as a combination of ∇log π(a) and ∇log π(b). Then subtract the constant b = 0.5 from both rewards and write it again. Which term changed?
predict.answer: Before: 0.75·1·∇log π(a) + 0.25·0·∇log π(b) = 0.75 ∇log π(a). After: 0.75·0.5·∇log π(a) − 0.25·0.5·∇log π(b). They are equal, because 0.25 ∇log π(b) = ∇π(b) = −∇π(a) = −0.75 ∇log π(a).
predict.why: Σ_o π(o) ∇log π(o) = ∇ Σ_o π(o) = 0, so the extra −b Σ π ∇log π term vanishes. The sampled estimate differs, the expectation does not.

transfer.q: Same two outputs, but now the coefficient is divided by a constant s = 0.4 that is the same for every output of this question (GRPO's group std plays this role; treat it here as a fixed number) instead of a constant being subtracted. Does the expected gradient direction stay the same as the un-scaled one, change direction, or only change magnitude? Explain in one clause.
choices: Direction can change, because s depends on the sampled rewards and does not factor out of the expectation
transfer.why: With a fixed s the factor leaves the expectation; the catch is that in GRPO s is recomputed per question from the sampled group, so across questions the effective learning rate differs (the course's p24 'upweights too easy or hard questions'). Within one question with s treated as a number, it is a pure rescaling.
transfer.varies: the operation on the coefficient: multiplicative rescaling instead of additive baseline
transfer.invariant: the expectation is over o ~ π with the score-function identity
transfer.distractor_from: Any rescaling of the coefficient is equally harmless; Subtracting a baseline changes the direction

retrieval.q: State the identity that makes subtracting a baseline b from the reward leave the expected policy gradient unchanged.
retrieval.answer: E_{o~π}[b ∇log π(o)] = b ∇ Σ_o π(o) = 0 for any b independent of o.

retrieval.q: In the unified policy-gradient form, what multiplies ∇_θ log π_θ(o_t | q, o_<t) inside the sum over tokens?
retrieval.answer: The gradient coefficient GC_A(q, o, t, π_rf), a per-token scalar set by the algorithm.

steps.why: This is the log-derivative trick, worked in full in lecture_16:policy-gradient-variance, applied here to one question q.
The policy is autoregressive, so the sequence score splits into one score per token, and each token can get its own weight.
Replace R by a per-token coefficient GC, which can hold the reward, a baseline or a KL term, and average over tokens. This is Eq. 5, the form every method in the paper takes.
b does not depend on the sampled output, so it leaves the expectation. Then π·∇log π = ∇π (lecture_16:baseline-validity-std-division works this in full).
The output probabilities of one question always sum to 1.

steps.do: The predict's two outputs, π(a) = 0.75 and π(b) = 0.25: 0.75·∇log π(a) + 0.25·∇log π(b) = ∇π(a) + ∇π(b) = 0. So subtracting 0.5 from both rewards removes 0.5 × 0 from the expected gradient.
steps.why: This is the identity in numbers. The baseline changes each sample's coefficient, and so the noise of a one-sample estimate, but not the expectation.

presentations.notice: The blue expected-gradient line stays flat however you move b; only the orange one-sample noise changes (it reaches 0 at b* = π(b)). Dividing by s rescales the blue line without changing its sign.

knowledge_points.label: Supplement: the ratio π_θ/π_old equals 1 at the first update, so clipping is inactive there
knowledge_points.statement: The surrogate's per-token ratio π_θ(o_t|·)/π_old(o_t|·) is exactly 1 when the gradient is taken at θ = θ_old; its gradient there is ∇log π_θ, the clip never binds, and with a single policy update per batch of samples the PPO/GRPO objective reduces to a plain policy gradient weighted by the advantage.

anchors.quote: it is assumed that the model only has a single update following each exploration stage, thereby ensuring that ... In this case, we can remove the $\min$ and ${\rm clip}$ operation
The policy model only has a single update following each exploration stage.
The gradient of $\mathcal{J}_{PPO}(\theta)$ is:
raw_logratio = (logprobs - old_logprobs).to(torch.float32) ... ratio        = torch.exp(logratio)
In the online case (rollout+immediate update), this is just policy gradient with group normalized rewards

provenance.filtering_note: The paper uses the ratio = 1 simplification only in the appendix to derive gradient coefficients, yet §4.2 says their actual runs also used a single update per exploration stage; put together (author inference) the min/clip of Eq. 3 never acted in the reported DeepSeekMath-RL training. The course says the same in one line on p18. FeynRL computes the ratio in float32 from stored old_logprobs and does run several updates per buffer, where clipping does act.

external_prerequisites.note: same supplement from the code side

misconceptions.belief: Because the ratio is 1, the ratio term contributes no gradient.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The value is 1 but its derivative is ∇π_θ/π_old = ∇log π_θ at θ = θ_old; the term is constant in value, not in slope.

misconceptions.belief: Clipping limits how far each single gradient step can move the policy.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Clipping only zeroes the gradient of tokens whose ratio has already left the band; on the first update no ratio has left it, so the first step is unclipped.

predict.q: At the moment the first gradient is computed after sampling, θ = θ_old. For one token with advantage Â = 0.8 and ε = 0.2, what are (i) the ratio, (ii) the value of min[ratio·Â, clip(ratio,1−ε,1+ε)·Â], and (iii) the gradient of that expression with respect to θ, written in terms of ∇log π_θ?
predict.answer: (i) 1; (ii) 0.8; (iii) 0.8 ∇log π_θ(o_t | q, o_<t): the unclipped branch is active and d(ratio)/dθ = ∇log π_θ at ratio 1.
predict.why: π_θ/π_old = 1 and 1 lies inside [0.8, 1.2], so min picks the unclipped term; its derivative is Â ∇(π_θ/π_old) = Â (π_θ/π_old) ∇log π_θ = Â ∇log π_θ (Eq. 17 with A_t = Â).

transfer.q: FeynRL runs several optimizer steps on the same replay buffer. After the first step a token's stored old_logprobs is −1.0 and the current logprobs is −0.5; Â = −1, clip band [0.8, 1.2]. Which branch of the min is active now, and what is the gradient from this token?
transfer.answer: ratio = e^{0.5} ≈ 1.65; unclipped = −1.65, clipped = 1.2·(−1) = −1.2; min = −1.65 (unclipped branch), so the gradient is −1.65 ∇log π_θ, not zero.
transfer.why: With a negative advantage the clip only protects the low side (ratio < 0.8): the clipped value −1.2 is larger than −1.65, so the minimum is the unclipped term and the policy keeps being pushed down on this token. This is the asymmetry the ratio-clip interactive shows.
transfer.varies: second update on the same samples (ratio no longer 1) and negative advantage
transfer.invariant: min over the two surrogates; clip is flat only outside the band on the side the advantage's sign selects

check.q: A run takes several optimizer steps per sampled batch, so the ratio has moved away from 1. For one token the stored old log-probability is −2.0 and the current log-probability is −2.3; its advantage is Â = +1 and the clip band is [0.8, 1.2]. The per-token surrogate is min[ρ·Â, clip(ρ, 0.8, 1.2)·Â] with ρ = π_θ/π_old. Its gradient with respect to θ is c·∇log π_θ for this token. What is c? Give it to three decimals. Type only the number.
check.why: ρ = exp(−2.3 − (−2.0)) = e^{−0.3} ≈ 0.741. Unclipped term = 0.741·1 = 0.741; clipped term = clip(0.741, 0.8, 1.2)·1 = 0.8. The min is 0.741, the unclipped branch, so the gradient is Â·∇ρ = Â·ρ·∇log π_θ = 0.741 ∇log π_θ. With a positive advantage the clip only binds on the high side (ρ > 1.2); a ratio below the band keeps its full gradient. Answering 0.8 treats the clip as limiting every step; answering 0 treats a moved ratio as gradient-free.
check.targets_misconception: Clipping limits how far each single gradient step can move the policy (so any ratio outside the band is cut off).
check.varies: Sign of the advantage flipped to positive and the ratio moved below the band instead of above it (functional: the other side of the clip asymmetry).
check.invariant: The min picks the unclipped branch unless the ratio has left the band in the direction the advantage pushes; d(ρ)/dθ = ρ·∇log π_θ.

retrieval.q: What is d/dθ of π_θ(o_t|·)/π_old(o_t|·) evaluated at θ = θ_old?
retrieval.answer: ∇_θ log π_θ(o_t | q, o_<t).

retrieval.q: Which two code lines in FeynRL produce the ratio from stored and current log-probabilities?

knowledge_points.label: Why PPO's value model is expensive for LLMs, and what GRPO replaces it with
knowledge_points.statement: PPO's advantage A_t comes from GAE over a learned value function V_ψ, which is typically a second model the size of the policy and must be accurate at every token although only the last token receives a reward; GRPO removes it and uses the mean reward of G outputs sampled for the same question as the baseline.

anchors.quote: As the value function employed in PPO is typically another model of comparable size as the policy model, it brings a substantial memory and computational burden.
usually only the last token is assigned a reward score by the reward model, which may complicate the training of a value function that is accurate at each token
uses the average reward of multiple sampled outputs, produced in response to the same question, as the baseline
GRPO foregoes the value model, instead estimating the baseline from group scores, significantly reducing training resources.
is the advantage, which is computed by applying Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (Schulman et al., 2015), based on the rewards
Value model (memory hungry, involves additional tuning for training)

provenance.filtering_note: The paper gives two reasons (memory/compute of a policy-sized critic; per-token value hard to learn from a last-token reward) and quantifies neither: no memory numbers, no ablation of PPO vs GRPO at equal compute appears in the paper. The course repeats the memory reason and adds 'complicated implementation' (p17). Basis: evidence for the claims, inference for any cost figure a learner derives.

external_prerequisites.note: one terminal reward is why a per-token value is hard

misconceptions.belief: GRPO is cheaper because it samples fewer outputs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It samples more (G = 64 per question in §4.2); the saving is the absent critic, both its memory and its forward/backward passes.

misconceptions.belief: Dropping the value model removes the reference model too.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Eq. 3 still needs π_ref for the KL term; GRPO holds policy, reference and reward model, PPO additionally holds the critic.

predict.q: RL fine-tuning of a 7B policy with PPO as described in §4.1.1 (policy, critic of comparable size, reference model, reward model). How many 7B-class networks are resident, and which one does GRPO remove?
predict.answer: Four under PPO; GRPO removes the critic (value function V_ψ), leaving three: policy, reference, reward model.
predict.why: The paper says the value function is 'typically another model of comparable size'; the reference model stays because Eq. 3's KL term needs it, and the reward model stays because it scores the outputs.

transfer.q: A team uses a rule-based verifier (exact-answer match) instead of a learned reward model, and sets β = 0 so no reference model is needed. Under PPO and under GRPO respectively, how many trained networks must be resident at training time?
transfer.answer: PPO: two (policy and critic). GRPO: one (policy only).
transfer.why: The reward model and reference model were removed by the setup change; the critic is specific to PPO's advantage estimate and is the one network GRPO never needs. This is the configuration FeynRL's gsm8k recipe runs (kl_coeff 0, rule reward).
transfer.varies: reward source (rule instead of model) and β = 0
transfer.invariant: PPO's advantage needs a critic; GRPO's does not

check.q: A team fine-tunes a 7B policy with RL. Assume every trained network costs 16 bytes per parameter (weights, gradients, Adam states) and every frozen network costs 2 bytes per parameter. Under PPO as in §4.1.1 they hold a trained policy, a trained value model of the same size, a frozen 7B reference model and a frozen 7B reward model. They switch to GRPO with the same reward model and the same β > 0. How many GB of model-state memory does the switch save (1 GB = 10^9 bytes)? Type only the number, in GB.
check.why: PPO: policy 7e9·16 = 112 GB, critic 112 GB, reference 7e9·2 = 14 GB, reward model 14 GB, total 252 GB. GRPO keeps policy, reference (β > 0 needs π_ref for the KL term in Eq. 3) and reward model: 112 + 14 + 14 = 140 GB. Saving = 252 − 140 = 112 GB, exactly the trained critic. Answering 126 also removes the reference model (wrong: Eq. 3 still needs it).
check.targets_misconception: Dropping the value model removes the reference model too.
check.varies: Asks for a memory figure under an explicit byte budget instead of a count of networks; reward and reference models are kept (domain: systems cost accounting).
check.invariant: GRPO removes exactly one network relative to PPO, the trained, policy-sized critic; reference and reward models stay whenever β > 0 and a learned reward is used.

retrieval.q: Name the two reasons the GRPO paper gives for not training a value function in the LLM setting.
retrieval.answer: It is another policy-sized model (memory and compute), and with a reward only on the last token a per-token value function is hard to train accurately.

retrieval.q: What does GRPO use as the baseline in place of the value function?
retrieval.answer: The average reward of the G outputs sampled for the same question.

knowledge_points.label: Group sampling and the outcome-supervised advantage: (r_i − mean) / std for every token
knowledge_points.statement: For each question GRPO samples G outputs from π_old, scores each with a scalar reward r_i, normalizes within the group, Ã_i = (r_i − mean(r)) / std(r), and under outcome supervision assigns that same number as the advantage Â_{i,t} of every token t of output o_i.

anchors.quote: these rewards are normalized by subtracting the group average and dividing by the group standard deviation
Outcome supervision provides the normalized reward at the end of each output
Compute $\hat{A}_{i,t}$ for the $t$ -th token of $o_{i}$ through group relative advantage estimation.
denom = len(samples) # number of samples in the group ... mean_scores = rewards_array.sum() / denom ... std_scores  = np.sqrt(((rewards_array - mean_scores)**2).sum() / max(denom - 1, 1))
zscore[-1] = (sample['token_rewards'][-1] - mean_scores) / (std_scores + 1e-8) ... if self.reward_broadcast: ... sample["token_zscores"][prompt_len:] = zscore[-1]
zscore is normalized rewards using the number of samples for each proompt (X -mu) / (std + eps) ... advs      = micro_batch['zscore'][:, :-1].to(device, non_blocking=True)
Calculate the advantage as “z-score within group”

provenance.filtering_note: The paper does not say whether std(r) divides by G or G−1, and adds no stability constant; FeynRL uses G−1 (Bessel) plus 1e-8, the course's nano-aha-moment example adds 1e-4 (p20). The paper also does not discuss the all-equal group (std = 0), where the formula is 0/0; implementations return 0 via the epsilon. The course further argues (p23-p24) that dividing by std is not a valid baseline and biases toward too-easy/too-hard questions; the paper does not raise this.

external_prerequisites.note: the same computation in normalize_rewards, with the Bessel and broadcast details
the course's critique of the std division

misconceptions.belief: Tokens late in a correct output get a larger advantage than early ones.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Under outcome supervision every token of o_i carries the identical Ã_i; token position matters only under process supervision.

misconceptions.belief: A correct output always receives a positive advantage.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The sign is relative to the group mean: if all G outputs are correct the advantage is 0, and a partially-credited output below the group mean is negative even if 'correct'.

predict.q: One question, G = 5, rewards [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]. Using the population standard deviation (divide by G), what advantage does every token of the correct output receive, and what do the tokens of each wrong output receive?
predict.answer: Correct output: +2.0 on every token; each wrong output: −0.5 on every token.
predict.why: mean = 0.2; deviations 0.8 and −0.2; variance (0.64 + 4·0.04)/5 = 0.16, std 0.4; 0.8/0.4 = 2.0 and −0.2/0.4 = −0.5. The five advantages sum to zero. (With G−1 as FeynRL does: +1.79 and −0.45.)
predict.targets_misconception: Tokens late in a correct output get a larger advantage than early ones.

transfer.q: A learned reward model gives graded scores instead of 0/1: G = 4, rewards [0.9, 0.1, 0.5, 0.5] (population std). Which outputs receive an advantage of exactly zero, and what is the advantage of the first output to two decimals?
transfer.answer: Outputs 3 and 4 (score 0.5 = group mean) get 0; output 1 gets (0.9 − 0.5)/0.283 ≈ +1.41 (output 2 gets −1.41).
transfer.why: Normalization is relative to the group: a score equal to the mean is neither reinforced nor penalized whatever its absolute value. std = sqrt((0.16 + 0.16 + 0 + 0)/4) = 0.283.
transfer.varies: graded rewards from a model instead of binary correctness; G = 4
transfer.invariant: advantage = (r_i − mean)/std over the group, identical for all tokens of an output

check.q: A reward gives 1.0 for a correct, well-formatted answer and 0.8 for a correct answer with bad formatting. For one question G = 4 outputs score [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.8]. Using GRPO outcome supervision with the population standard deviation (divide by G), what advantage does the 200th token of output 4 receive? Give it to two decimals. Type only the number.
check.why: mean = 3.8/4 = 0.95; deviations 0.05, 0.05, 0.05, −0.15; population variance = (3·0.0025 + 0.0225)/4 = 0.0075; std = 0.0866. Ã_4 = (0.8 − 0.95)/0.0866 = −1.732. Under outcome supervision every token of o_4, including the 200th, carries this same value. Output 4 is correct yet negative because it sits below the group mean.
check.targets_misconception: A correct output always receives a positive advantage (and token position changes the advantage).
check.varies: Rewards encode a formatting bonus so a correct output is below the mean; asks about a specific late token (domain: reward design).
check.invariant: Ã_i = (r_i − mean(r))/std(r) is relative to the group and is broadcast unchanged to every token of o_i.

retrieval.q: Write the outcome-supervised GRPO advantage for token t of output o_i.
retrieval.answer: Â_{i,t} = (r_i − mean(r)) / std(r), the same for all t.

retrieval.q: Over the G outputs of one question, what is the sum of the GRPO advantages?
retrieval.answer: Zero, because the group mean was subtracted.

retrieval.q: Which two details of the std in the group advantage does the paper leave unspecified, so that implementations such as FeynRL and nano-aha-moment fill them in differently?
retrieval.answer: Whether the variance divides by G or G−1, and the stability constant added to the std.

steps.do: Outcome supervision: Â_{i,t} = r̃_i for every token t of o_i. Every token of the correct output gets +2.0, and every token of each wrong output gets −0.5.
steps.why: The reward arrives only at the end of the output, so the paper gives that one normalized number to all of its tokens (§4.1.2).

knowledge_points.label: Process supervision: per-step rewards, normalized over all steps, summed from step t onward
knowledge_points.statement: With a process reward model each reasoning step's final token gets a reward r_i^{index(j)}; all step rewards of all G outputs are normalized by their common mean and std, and a token's advantage is the sum of the normalized rewards of the steps that end at or after it, Â_{i,t} = Σ_{index(j) ≥ t} r̃_i^{index(j)}, so earlier tokens accumulate more terms.

anchors.quote: we also explore process supervision, which provides a reward at the end of each reasoning step
the process supervision calculates the advantage of each token as the sum of the normalized rewards from the following steps
Outcome supervision only provides a reward at the end of each output, which may not be sufficient and efficient to supervise the policy in complex mathematical tasks.
with some gains from process supervision

provenance.filtering_note: The normalization is over the pooled set R of all steps of all outputs (not per output and not per step index), and the sum is a reward-to-go without discounting. The paper reports GRPO+PS above GRPO+OS only as curves (Fig. 5); the course mentions 'some gains' (p21) and otherwise skips process supervision. FeynRL does not implement per-token rewards (rollouts/base.py raises on is_per_token).

misconceptions.belief: Process supervision normalizes each step's reward against the other outputs' same-numbered step.
misconceptions.why_wrong: §4.1.3 pools every step reward of every output into one set R and uses its mean and std; step indices are not aligned across outputs.

misconceptions.belief: Under process supervision all tokens of a step share the advantage of that step only.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A token's advantage sums the normalized rewards of its own step and every later step; the last step's tokens have one term, the first step's tokens have K_i terms.

predict.q: An output has three steps whose normalized step rewards are r̃^{(1)} = +0.5, r̃^{(2)} = −1.0, r̃^{(3)} = +0.8. What advantage do tokens in step 1, step 2 and step 3 receive under process supervision?
predict.answer: Step 1 tokens: 0.5 − 1.0 + 0.8 = +0.3; step 2 tokens: −1.0 + 0.8 = −0.2; step 3 tokens: +0.8.
predict.why: Â_{i,t} sums the normalized rewards of every step ending at or after t (reward-to-go, no discount). Earlier tokens are credited for what follows them.
predict.targets_misconception: Under process supervision all tokens of a step share the advantage of that step only.

transfer.q: Compare two outputs for the same question under outcome supervision versus process supervision: both end with the correct answer (outcome reward 1), but output B contains a wrong intermediate step that it later corrects. Under which scheme can B's early tokens receive a different advantage from A's, and in what direction for the tokens of the wrong step?
transfer.answer: Only under process supervision; the wrong step's tokens in B get a lower (more negative) advantage because that step's normalized reward is low and it is included in their sum, while under outcome supervision every token of A and B gets the identical normalized outcome reward.
transfer.why: Outcome supervision cannot see inside the output; process supervision assigns each step a reward and the token advantage accumulates from that step forward, so a bad step lowers its own and all earlier tokens' advantage.
transfer.varies: the supervision scheme, with the final answer held fixed
transfer.invariant: advantage is still a group-normalized reward; only the granularity of the reward and the summation differ

check.q: Process supervision with G = 2 outputs for one question. A process reward model gives raw step rewards: output A has 2 steps scoring [0.9, 0.5]; output B has 3 steps scoring [0.2, 0.6, 0.8]. Normalize as in §4.1.3, using the population standard deviation (divide by the number of rewards normalized). What advantage does a token inside the first step of output B receive? Give it to two decimals. Type only the number.
check.why: §4.1.3 pools all step rewards R = {0.9, 0.5, 0.2, 0.6, 0.8}: mean = 0.6, population variance = (0.09 + 0.01 + 0.16 + 0 + 0.04)/5 = 0.06, std = 0.2449. misconceptions.belief: RFT and GRPO differ because GRPO samples more outputs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Both sample multiple outputs per question; in the paradigm they differ in data source (frozen SFT vs live policy) and coefficient (I(o) vs Â + KL).

misconceptions.belief: A wrong output contributes nothing under either method.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Under RFT/Online RFT its coefficient is 0; under GRPO it carries a negative Â and is actively pushed down ('penalization').

predict.q: Two methods see the same question with 4 sampled outputs, all correct. Online RFT applies GC = I(o); GRPO applies GC = Â (ignore the KL term). What coefficient does each method put on the tokens of these outputs, and which method moves the policy on this question?
predict.answer: Online RFT: 1 on every token, so it keeps pushing up the probability of these outputs. GRPO: Â = 0 for all four, so it does not move the policy on this question.
predict.why: I(o) is absolute (correct = 1); Â is relative to the group. A question the policy already always solves gives GRPO no signal, which is why difficulty filtering matters for GRPO-style training.
predict.targets_misconception: RFT and GRPO differ because GRPO samples more outputs.

transfer.q: Reverse the case: 4 outputs, all wrong. What coefficient does Online RFT put on them, what does GRPO put on them, and which method 'learns from negative gradients' here?
transfer.answer: Online RFT: 0 on all tokens (nothing learned). GRPO: Â = 0 as well, because the group is uniform; neither method learns from this question. Negative gradients appear in GRPO only when the group is mixed, where the wrong outputs get Â < 0.
transfer.why: The group-relative coefficient needs variation inside the group; a uniformly failing group is as uninformative to GRPO as a uniformly succeeding one. The 'negative gradient' advantage over RFT is specific to mixed groups.
transfer.varies: the group outcome (all wrong instead of all correct)

check.q: Three questions, 4 outputs each, binary reward 1 for correct and 0 for wrong: question X has 4 correct outputs, question Y has 4 wrong outputs, question Z has 1 correct and 3 wrong. Under GRPO with group-normalized Â (ignore the KL term), on how many of the 12 outputs are the tokens given a negative coefficient? Type only the number.
check.why: X and Y are uniform groups: r_i − mean = 0 for every output, so Â = 0 (not negative) for all 8. In Z, mean = 0.25; the correct output gets (1 − 0.25)/std > 0 and each wrong output gets (0 − 0.25)/std < 0. So exactly the 3 wrong outputs of Z are pushed down. Counting Y's wrong outputs too gives 7; Online RFT would give 0 negatives.
check.targets_misconception: A wrong output is always pushed down by GRPO (or contributes nothing under either method).
check.varies: Mixes uniform-correct, uniform-wrong and mixed groups in one batch and asks for a count (functional: aggregate over group types).
check.invariant: GRPO's coefficient is nonzero only when the group's rewards vary; negative gradients come from below-mean outputs of mixed groups.

retrieval.q: Which two methods in the unified paradigm share the same gradient coefficient and differ only in data source?
retrieval.answer: RFT (outputs from π_sft, offline) and Online RFT (outputs from π_θ, online).

retrieval.q: What single property of its gradient coefficient makes GRPO different from Online RFT?
retrieval.answer: GRPO adjusts the gradient coefficient by the reward value, allowing differential reinforcement and penalization; Online RFT uses a 0/1 coefficient.

predict.why: 1024 questions × G = 64 outputs = 65,536 outputs; at max length 1024 that is up to 67,108,864 generated tokens per batch. The rollout cost, not the critic, is where GRPO spends compute.

misconceptions.belief: RL trained only on GSM8K/MATH chain-of-thought should not change tool-integrated or Chinese benchmarks.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Table 5 shows gains on every printed out-of-domain column; the authors use this as evidence that RL generalizes beyond its training questions.

predict.q: RL used only GSM8K/MATH chain-of-thought questions. Before looking at Table 5: did the Chinese benchmarks (MGSM-zh, CMATH) and the tool-integrated MATH score go up, go down, or stay flat for DeepSeekMath-RL vs Instruct? Give the direction and one printed number.

transfer.q: A model solves a given MATH problem in 10 of 64 samples before RL and in 40 of 64 after. Which of Pass@64 and Maj@64 for this problem can change, and in which direction? Then say which metric the paper found RL to improve overall and what that implies about problems solved in 0 of 64 samples before RL.
transfer.answer: Pass@64 is 1 both times (unchanged); Maj@64 can flip from wrong to right because the correct answer now dominates the vote. The paper found Maj@K improved and Pass@K did not, implying problems with 0/64 before RL mostly stayed at 0 after: RL re-weighted the distribution over answers it could already produce.
transfer.why: Pass@K asks whether any sample is right, Maj@K whether the plurality is; concentrating probability on an already-reachable answer moves the second without the first. That is the mechanism behind §5.2.2's reading.
transfer.varies: a single problem's sample counts instead of a benchmark aggregate

check.q: Five MATH problems, 8 samples each. Correct samples per problem before RL: [0, 2, 3, 6, 1]; after RL: [0, 5, 7, 8, 3]. Count a problem as solved under Maj@8 when more than half (at least 5) of its 8 samples are correct, and under Pass@8 when at least one is. By how many percentage points does Maj@8 accuracy over the five problems change from before to after RL? Type only the number of points.
check.why: Maj@8 here is simplified to 'at least 5 of 8 correct'. Maj@8 before: only the problem with 6/8 qualifies, 1/5 = 20%. After: 5/8, 7/8, 8/8 qualify, 3/5 = 60%. Change = +40 points. Pass@8 is 4/5 = 80% both before and after (the 0/8 problem stays at 0), the pattern Fig. 7 reports: RL concentrates probability on answers the model could already reach, so Maj@K rises while Pass@K stays flat.
check.targets_misconception: A higher Maj@K means the model can now solve problems it could not solve before.
check.varies: A five-problem tally with a stated majority rule replaces the single-problem qualitative case (modality: computed metric from sample counts).
check.invariant: Maj@K rewards how often the correct answer is sampled; Pass@K only whether it is sampled at all; re-weighting moves the first, not the second.

retrieval.q: Give DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B and DeepSeekMath-RL 7B chain-of-thought accuracies on GSM8K and MATH.
Which metric did RL improve and which did it leave unchanged, and what did the authors conclude from that?
retrieval.answer: Maj@K improved, Pass@K did not; they concluded RL makes the output distribution more robust (boosts the correct answer within the top-K) rather than adding fundamental capability.
